[0] A specially appointed judge has sided with Apple as it tries to compel 14 federal agencies to hand over documents as part of its defense in the Justice Department’s antitrust lawsuit. Here are the details.

[1] A little background

[2] Last May, Apple asked the court overseeing the Justice Department’s antitrust case against the company, filed in 2024, to force the following 14 federal agencies to hand over documents about how they evaluate, purchase, and use smartphones and wearables:

  • [3] Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)
  • [4] Department of Commerce
  • [5] Department of Homeland Security
  • [6] Department of Defense
  • [7] Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)
  • [8] Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
  • [9] General Services Administration
  • [10] Department of Labor
  • [11] National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
  • [12] National Security Agency (NSA)
  • [13] Office of the Director of National Intelligence
  • [14] Office of Management and Budget
  • [15] Office of Personnel Management
  • [16] Department of State

[17] Apple argued in its motion that these records could help support its defense against allegations that its iPhone policies are anticompetitive.

[18] In short, Apple’s argument is that if federal agencies choose its products because of their security, privacy, or other features, that supports its claim that the disputed practices are legitimate product benefits rather than anticompetitive restrictions.

[19] However, the government pushed back against Apple’s request, arguing that these agencies are unrelated to the case, don’t regulate smartphones, and don’t purchase or use them the way ordinary consumers do.

[20] The government asked the court to block the subpoenas, claiming they were irrelevant and overly burdensome, and pointed out that they could involve privileged, confidential, or national security-related information.

[21] The court subsequently referred the dispute to retired federal judge Jose Linares, who, serving as a special discovery master, is responsible for deciding whether Apple can enforce the subpoenas.

[22] In complex cases involving extensive discovery, courts sometimes appoint special masters to resolve narrower disputes, easing the workload of the judge handling the broader case. A special master can be a retired judge, a practicing attorney, or another expert with relevant experience.

[23] Apple allowed to continue seeking documents from federal agencies

[24] Judge Linares has now sided with Apple, ruling that all of its document requests are relevant to the core allegations in the case. He also said the government had failed to provide sufficient justification for its broad objections.

[27] Although the special discovery master sided with Apple, that doesn’t mean the company will immediately get every document it requested.

[28] Instead, agencies can still withhold specific records they believe are privileged or otherwise protected, but they must list those claimed privileged records in a privilege log. Any disputes over those claims could trigger a new round of discovery fights, possibly including in-camera review by Judge Linares.
